questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two point charges $+8q$ and $-2q$ are located at $x=0$ and $x=L$ respectively. What is the location of a point on the x-axis from the origin, at which the net electric field due to these two point charges is zero?
questions.solution:
Let the point where the net electric field is zero be at a distance $x$ from the origin on the x-axis.

Since the charges have opposite signs, the null point must lie outside the region between the charges and closer to the charge with the smaller magnitude. Thus, the point lies at $x \gt L$.

Equating the magnitudes of the electric fields due to both charges at this point:

$\dfrac{k(8q)}{x^2} = \dfrac{k(2q)}{(x-L)^2}$

$\dfrac{4}{x^2} = \dfrac{1}{(x-L)^2}$

Taking the square root on both sides:

$\dfrac{2}{x} = \dfrac{1}{x-L}$

$2x - 2L = x$

$x = 2L$

Answer: $2L$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three point charges $q_1 = 1\ \mu\text{C}$, $q_2 = -2\ \mu\text{C}$, and $q_3 = 3\ \mu\text{C}$ are placed at $(1, 0, 0)$, $(0, 2, 0)$ and $(0, 0, 3)$ respectively. The electric potential at origin is $\left\{\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9\ \text{SI unit}\right\}$
questions.solution:
The electric potential at the origin is given by the superposition principle:

$V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \left( \dfrac{q_1}{r_1} + \dfrac{q_2}{r_2} + \dfrac{q_3}{r_3} \right)$

The distances of the charges from the origin are:

$r_1 = \sqrt{1^2 + 0^2 + 0^2} = 1\ \text{m}$

$r_2 = \sqrt{0^2 + 2^2 + 0^2} = 2\ \text{m}$

$r_3 = \sqrt{0^2 + 0^2 + 3^2} = 3\ \text{m}$

Substituting the values of charges and distances:

$V = 9 \times 10^9 \left( \dfrac{1 \times 10^{-6}}{1} + \dfrac{-2 \times 10^{-6}}{2} + \dfrac{3 \times 10^{-6}}{3} \right)$

$V = 9 \times 10^9 \times 10^{-6} (1 - 1 + 1)$

$V = 9 \times 10^3\ \text{V}$

Answer: $9 \times 10^3\ \text{V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three electric charges $2q$, $2q$, $-4q$ are placed at the corners of equilateral triangle of side $'x'$. The magnitude of electric dipole moment of the system is
questions.solution:
The system of charges can be considered as two dipoles by splitting the $-4q$ charge into two charges of $-2q$ each.

One dipole is formed by $-2q$ and $2q$ along one side of the equilateral triangle, having a dipole moment $p_1 = (2q)x = 2qx$.

The second dipole is formed by the other $-2q$ and $2q$ along the adjacent side, having a dipole moment $p_2 = (2q)x = 2qx$.

The angle between the two dipole moment vectors is $60^{\circ}$, which is the interior angle of the equilateral triangle.

The magnitude of the resultant dipole moment is given by:

$p_{net} = \sqrt{p_1^2 + p_2^2 + 2p_1p_2\cos 60^{\circ}}$

Substituting $p_1 = p_2 = 2qx$ and $\cos 60^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{2}$:

$p_{net} = \sqrt{(2qx)^2 + (2qx)^2 + 2(2qx)(2qx)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}$

$p_{net} = \sqrt{4q^2x^2 + 4q^2x^2 + 4q^2x^2}$

$p_{net} = \sqrt{12q^2x^2} = 2\sqrt{3}qx$

Answer: $2\sqrt{3}qx$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Pressure exerted by an ideal gas on the walls of the container is equal to
a) mean kinetic energy per unit volume.
b) half of mean kinetic energy per unit volume.
c) one-third of mean kinetic energy per unit volume.
d) two-third of mean kinetic energy per unit volume.
questions.solution:
The pressure exerted by an ideal gas is given by $P = \dfrac{1}{3} \rho v_{rms}^2$, where $\rho$ is the density of the gas and $v_{rms}$ is the root mean square velocity.

The mean kinetic energy per unit volume is given by $E = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_{rms}^2$.

From these two equations, we can write $P = \dfrac{2}{3} \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_{rms}^2 \right) = \dfrac{2}{3} E$.

Therefore, the pressure exerted by an ideal gas is equal to two-thirds of the mean kinetic energy per unit volume.

Answer: d

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The pressure $P$, volume $V$ and temperature $T$ of a gas in the jar A and the other gas in the jar B is at pressure $2P$, volume $V/4$ and temperature $2T$, then the ratio of the number of molecules in the jar A and B will be
questions.solution:
Using the ideal gas equation, $PV = NkT$, where $N$ is the number of molecules.

For jar A:
$N_A = \dfrac{PV}{kT}$

For jar B:
$N_B = \dfrac{P_B V_B}{k T_B} = \dfrac{(2P)(V/4)}{k(2T)} = \dfrac{PV/2}{2kT} = \dfrac{PV}{4kT}$

Ratio of number of molecules:
$\dfrac{N_A}{N_B} = \dfrac{\dfrac{PV}{kT}}{\dfrac{PV}{4kT}} = \dfrac{4}{1}$

The ratio is $4 : 1$.

Answer: $4 : 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a cyclotron, a charged particle
options: speeds up between the dees because of the magnetic field.
slows down within a dee and speeds up between the dees.
questions.solution:
Inside the dees of a cyclotron, a uniform magnetic field acts perpendicular to the velocity of the charged particle. This magnetic field provides the necessary centripetal force, causing the particle to move in a circular path. Since the direction of velocity continuously changes, the particle experiences centripetal acceleration.

In the gap between the dees, an oscillating electric field is present. This electric field increases the speed (and kinetic energy) of the particle, which is also a form of acceleration (tangential acceleration).

Therefore, the charged particle undergoes acceleration all the time.

Answer: undergoes acceleration all the time.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The magnetic flux near the axis and inside the air core solenoid of length $60\ \text{cm}$ carrying current $'I'$ is $1.57 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{Wb}$. Its magnetic moment will be $\{$cross-sectional area of a solenoid is very small as compared to its length, $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \text{SI unit}\}$
questions.solution:
The magnetic field inside a long solenoid is given by:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{L}$

where $N$ is the total number of turns, $I$ is the current, and $L$ is the length of the solenoid.

The magnetic flux through the cross-section of the solenoid is:

$\Phi = B A = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I A}{L}$

The magnetic moment of a solenoid is given by:

$M = N I A$

Substituting $M$ into the flux equation, we get:

$\Phi = \dfrac{\mu_0 M}{L}$

Rearranging to solve for the magnetic moment $M$:

$M = \dfrac{\Phi L}{\mu_0}$

Given values are:
$\Phi = 1.57 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{Wb}$
$L = 60\ \text{cm} = 0.6\ \text{m}$
$\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \text{T m/A} = 4 \times 3.14 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{T m/A} = 12.56 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{T m/A}$

Substituting these values into the formula:

$M = \dfrac{1.57 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.6}{12.56 \times 10^{-7}}$

$M = \dfrac{1.57}{12.56} \times 0.6 \times 10$

$M = \dfrac{1}{8} \times 6 = \dfrac{3}{4} = 0.75\ \text{A m}^2$

Answer: $0.75\ \text{Am}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A magnetizing field of $360\ \text{A/m}$ produces a magnetic flux density $B = 0.6\ \text{T}$ in a ferromagnetic material. The permeability of the material in T-m/A is
questions.solution:
Given, magnetizing field $H = 360\ \text{A/m}$

Magnetic flux density $B = 0.6\ \text{T}$

The permeability of the material is given by the relation $\mu = \dfrac{B}{H}$

Substituting the given values, we get

$\mu = \dfrac{0.6}{360} = \dfrac{1}{600}\ \text{T-m/A}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{600}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the relation between the two vectors $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = \hat{i} + \dfrac{5}{2}\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$ ?
questions.solution:
Given vectors are $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = \hat{i} + \dfrac{5}{2}\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$.

Taking $2$ common from the components of $\vec{A}$:

$\vec{A} = 2(\hat{i} + \dfrac{5}{2}\hat{j} - 3\hat{k})$

$\vec{A} = 2\vec{B}$

Since $\vec{A}$ is a scalar multiple of $\vec{B}$, the two vectors are parallel.

Answer: $\vec{A}$ is parallel to $\vec{B}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The error in measurement of radius of sphere is $0.2\ \%$, then the percentage error in its volume is
questions.solution:
The volume of a sphere is given by $V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$

Taking relative error on both sides, we get $\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = 3 \dfrac{\Delta r}{r}$

Percentage error in volume is $\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} \times 100 = 3 \left(\dfrac{\Delta r}{r} \times 100\right)$

Given percentage error in radius is $0.2\ \%$

Therefore, percentage error in volume $= 3 \times 0.2\ \% = 0.6\ \%$

Answer: $0.6\ \%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block is kept on the floor of an elevator at rest. The elevator starts descending with acceleration of $5\ \text{m/s}^2$. The displacement of the block during the first $0.2\ \text{s}$ after the start is $\{$Take $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2\}$
questions.solution:
The acceleration of the elevator is $a = 5\ \text{m/s}^2$ downwards.

Since the downward acceleration of the elevator is less than the acceleration due to gravity ($a \lt g$), the block does not lose contact with the floor of the elevator. Thus, the acceleration of the block is the same as that of the elevator, $a = 5\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Using the second equation of motion for the displacement of the block with initial velocity $u = 0$ and time $t = 0.2\ \text{s}$:

$s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$

$s = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times (0.2)^2$

$s = 2.5 \times 0.04$

$s = 0.1\ \text{m}$

Converting the displacement into centimeters:

$s = 0.1 \times 100\ \text{cm} = 10\ \text{cm}$

Answer: $10\ \text{cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When a nucleus in an atom undergoes a radioactive decay, the atomic number and/or mass number of the atom
options: do not change for any type of radioactivity.
change for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ radiations but not for $\gamma$ radiation.
change for $\alpha$ radiation but not for others.
change for $\beta$ radiation but not for others.
questions.solution:
In $\alpha$ decay, the atomic number decreases by $2$ and the mass number decreases by $4$.

In $\beta$ decay, the atomic number changes by $1$ (increases in $\beta^{-}$ and decreases in $\beta^{+}$) while the mass number remains unchanged.

In $\gamma$ decay, neither the atomic number nor the mass number changes, as it only involves a transition between nuclear energy levels.

Thus, the atomic number and/or mass number change for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ radiations but not for $\gamma$ radiation.

Answer: change for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ radiations but not for $\gamma$ radiation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The periodic time of a simple pendulum, (the simple pendulum with its bob is in air) is T. But if the bob of the simple pendulum is completely immersed in a non viscous liquid, whose density is $\dfrac{1}{20}$ times the density of material of the bob, then its new period will be
questions.solution:
The time period of a simple pendulum in air is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$.

When the bob is immersed in a liquid, the effective acceleration due to gravity $g'$ becomes:

$g' = g \left(1 - \dfrac{\rho}{\sigma}\right)$

where $\rho$ is the density of the liquid and $\sigma$ is the density of the material of the bob.

Given that $\rho = \dfrac{\sigma}{20}$, we have:

$g' = g \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{20}\right) = \dfrac{19g}{20}$

The new time period $T'$ is:

$T' = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g'}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{\dfrac{19g}{20}}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}} \sqrt{\dfrac{20}{19}}$

$T' = \sqrt{\dfrac{20}{19}} T$

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{20}{19}}T$

questions.q: The graph shows variation of displacement of a particle performing SHM with time t. which of the following statements is correct from the graph?
options: The acceleration is maximum at time $T$.
The force is maximum at time $\dfrac{3T}{4}$.
The velocity is zero at time $\dfrac{T}{2}$.
The kinetic energy is equal to total energy at time $\dfrac{T}{4}$.
questions.solution:
From the given graph, the displacement of the particle is $x = A \sin(\omega t)$, where $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$.

At $t = T$, displacement $x = 0$. Acceleration $a = -\omega^2 x = 0$. Thus, acceleration is zero.

At $t = \dfrac{3T}{4}$, displacement $x = -A$ (extreme position). The restoring force is $F = -kx$. The magnitude of force is $|F| = k|-A| = kA$, which is the maximum value. Thus, the force is maximum.

At $t = \dfrac{T}{2}$, displacement $x = 0$ (mean position). Velocity is maximum at the mean position, not zero.

At $t = \dfrac{T}{4}$, displacement $x = A$ (extreme position). Velocity is zero, so kinetic energy is zero. Total energy is entirely potential energy.

Answer: The force is maximum at time $\dfrac{3T}{4}$.

questions.q: The frequency of small oscillations of thin uniform vertical rod of mass $'m'$ and length $'l'$ hinged at point O with the help of two springs with spring constants $k_1$ and $k_2$, is
questions.solution:
Let the rod be displaced by a small angle $\theta$ from the vertical.

The horizontal displacement of the lower end of the rod is $x = l\theta$.

The restoring force exerted by the two springs is $F = (k_1 + k_2)x = (k_1 + k_2)l\theta$.

The restoring torque due to the springs about the hinge O is:
$\tau_s = -F \cdot l = -(k_1 + k_2)l^2\theta$

The center of mass of the rod is at a distance $\dfrac{l}{2}$ from the hinge O. The restoring torque due to gravity about O is:
$\tau_g = -mg \left(\dfrac{l}{2}\right) \sin\theta \approx -\dfrac{mgl}{2}\theta$

The total restoring torque on the rod is:
$\tau = \tau_s + \tau_g = -\left[ (k_1 + k_2)l^2 + \dfrac{mgl}{2} \right]\theta$

The moment of inertia of the uniform rod about the hinge O is $I = \dfrac{ml^2}{3}$.

Using the equation of motion $\tau = I\alpha$:
$\dfrac{ml^2}{3}\alpha = -\left[ (k_1 + k_2)l^2 + \dfrac{mgl}{2} \right]\theta$

$\alpha = -\left[ \dfrac{3(k_1 + k_2)}{m} + \dfrac{3g}{2l} \right]\theta$

Comparing this with the standard equation for simple harmonic motion $\alpha = -\omega^2\theta$, the angular frequency is:
$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{3(k_1 + k_2)}{m} + \dfrac{3g}{2l}}$

The frequency of oscillation is:
$f = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\dfrac{3(k_1 + k_2)}{m} + \dfrac{3g}{2l}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\dfrac{3(k_1 + k_2)}{m} + \dfrac{3g}{2l}}$

questions.q: The refracting angle of a prism is $'A'$ and its refractive index is $\cot\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)$. The minimum deviation produced by the prism is
questions.solution:
The refractive index of a prism is given by the formula:

$\mu = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}$

Given that $\mu = \cot\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)$, we can write:

$\cot\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\cos\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}$

Equating the two expressions for $\mu$:

$\dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)} = \dfrac{\cos\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}$

$\sin\left(\dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right) = \cos\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)$

Using the trigonometric identity $\cos(\theta) = \sin(90^{\circ} - \theta)$, we get:

$\sin\left(\dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right) = \sin\left(90^{\circ} - \dfrac{A}{2}\right)$

Equating the angles:

$\dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2} = 90^{\circ} - \dfrac{A}{2}$

$A + \delta_m = 180^{\circ} - A$

$\delta_m = 180^{\circ} - 2A$

Answer: $(180)^\circ - 2A$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In case of semiconductors, the band gap between the valence band and conduction band is
options: $1\ \text{eV}$ or less but greater than zero.
questions.solution:
In solid-state physics, materials are classified into conductors, insulators, and semiconductors based on the size of the forbidden energy gap ($E_g$) between the valence band and the conduction band.

For conductors, the valence band and conduction band overlap, so the band gap is zero.

For insulators, the forbidden energy gap is very large, typically greater than $3$ eV to $5$ eV, making it extremely difficult for electrons to jump to the conduction band.

For semiconductors, the forbidden energy gap is small but non-zero, usually around $1$ eV or less. For example, the band gap for Silicon is approximately $1.1$ eV and for Germanium is approximately $0.7$ eV at room temperature.

Therefore, the band gap in semiconductors is $1$ eV or less but greater than zero.

Answer: $1\ \text{eV}$ or less but greater than zero.

The output of the first NAND gate with inputs $A$ and $B$ is:
$Y = \overline{A \cdot B}$

This output $Y$ is connected to both inputs of the second NAND gate. A NAND gate with its inputs tied together acts as a NOT gate.

The final output $X$ is:
$X = \overline{Y \cdot Y} = \overline{Y}$

Substituting the value of $Y$:
$X = \overline{\overline{A \cdot B}} = A \cdot B$

Thus, the circuit acts as an AND gate.

questions.q: To emit red or green light, LED is manufactured using
questions.solution:
Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs) require semiconductors with a specific band gap to emit visible light (typically between $1.8\text{ eV}$ and $3.0\text{ eV}$).

The compound semiconductor Gallium Arsenic Phosphide ($GaAs_{1-x}P_x$) is widely used for manufacturing LEDs of various colours. The emission wavelength depends on the band gap, which can be tuned by varying the composition ratio of Arsenic to Phosphorus ($x$).

For instance, $GaAs_{0.6}P_{0.4}$ has a band gap of approximately $1.9\text{ eV}$ and is used to emit red light. By increasing the phosphorus content, the band gap increases, allowing the LED to emit higher-energy visible light, such as green.

Therefore, Gallium Arsenic Phosphide is used to manufacture LEDs that emit red or green light.

Answer: gallium arsenic phosphide.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If two temperatures differ by $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$ on Celsius scale, the difference in temperature on Fahrenheit scale is
questions.solution:
The relation between temperature on Celsius scale and Fahrenheit scale is given by

$F = \dfrac{9}{5}C + 32$

For a change in temperature, the relation becomes

$\Delta F = \dfrac{9}{5}\Delta C$

Given $\Delta C = 25^\circ\text{C}$, substituting this value gives

$\Delta F = \dfrac{9}{5} \times 25 = 45^\circ\text{F}$

Answer: $45\ \text{F}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The ratio of emissive power of perfectly black body at $1327\ ^\circ\text{C}$ to that at $527\ ^\circ\text{C}$ is
questions.solution:
According to Stefan-Boltzmann law, the emissive power of a perfectly black body is given by $E = \sigma T^4$, where $T$ is the absolute temperature.

Converting the given temperatures to Kelvin:
$T_1 = 1327^\circ\text{C} + 273 = 1600\text{ K}$
$T_2 = 527^\circ\text{C} + 273 = 800\text{ K}$

The ratio of their emissive powers is:
$\dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = \left(\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^4$

Substituting the values:
$\dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = \left(\dfrac{1600}{800}\right)^4 = (2)^4 = 16$

The ratio is $16 : 1$.

Answer: $16 : 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The work done by an ideal gas during closed cycle $1 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow 3 \rightarrow 4 \rightarrow 1$ as shown in figure is
questions.solution:
The total work done by the gas is the algebraic sum of the work done in the two separate loops shown in the $P-V$ diagram.

From the indicated arrows, the lower loop is traversed in a clockwise direction. Thus, the work done in this loop is positive and equal to the area of the lower triangle.

$W_1 = +\dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = +\dfrac{1}{2} \times (5V_0 - V_0) \times (3P_0 - P_0)$

$W_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4V_0 \times 2P_0 = 4P_0V_0$

The upper loop is traversed in a counter-clockwise direction. Thus, the work done in this loop is negative and equal to the negative of the area of the upper triangle.

The upper and lower triangles are similar because their bases are parallel. The ratio of their heights is $\dfrac{4P_0 - 3P_0}{3P_0 - P_0} = \dfrac{P_0}{2P_0} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Therefore, the base of the upper triangle is half the base of the lower triangle, which is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 4V_0 = 2V_0$.

$W_2 = -\dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = -\dfrac{1}{2} \times 2V_0 \times (4P_0 - 3P_0)$

$W_2 = -\dfrac{1}{2} \times 2V_0 \times P_0 = -P_0V_0$

The net work done during the complete cycle is $W = W_1 + W_2 = 4P_0V_0 - P_0V_0 = 3P_0V_0$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Which of the following statements is NOT CORRECT?
In an isothermal process,
a. there is perfect thermal equilibrium with environment.
b. there is no change in internal energy during the process.
c. the work done is equal to zero.
d. the time taken is very large.
questions.solution:
In an isothermal process, the temperature of the system remains constant, which means $\Delta T = 0$.

For an ideal gas, the internal energy depends only on temperature, so the change in internal energy $\Delta U = 0$.

To maintain a constant temperature, the process must be carried out very slowly so that the system remains in perfect thermal equilibrium with its surroundings. Thus, the time taken for the process is very large.

According to the first law of thermodynamics, $\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$. Since $\Delta U = 0$, we have $\Delta Q = \Delta W$. The work done in an isothermal process is given by $W = nRT \ln\left(\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\right)$, which is not zero unless the volume is also constant.

Therefore, the statement that the work done is equal to zero is incorrect.

Answer: c

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In Young's double slit experiment, the slits are $2\ \text{mm}$ apart and are illuminated by photons of two wavelengths $\lambda_1 = 6000\ Å$ and $\lambda_2 = 5000\ Å$ one after the other. At what minimum distance from the common central bright fringe on the screen $2\ \text{m}$ from the slit will, a bright fringe from one interference pattern coincide with a bright fringe from the other?
questions.solution:
Given:
$d = 2\ \text{mm} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}$
$D = 2\ \text{m}$
$\lambda_1 = 6000\ \text{\AA} = 6 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}$
$\lambda_2 = 5000\ \text{\AA} = 5 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}$

Let the $n_1$-th bright fringe of $\lambda_1$ coincide with the $n_2$-th bright fringe of $\lambda_2$. The position of the $n$-th bright fringe from the central maximum is given by $y = \dfrac{n \lambda D}{d}$.

For coincidence:
$\dfrac{n_1 \lambda_1 D}{d} = \dfrac{n_2 \lambda_2 D}{d}$

$n_1 \lambda_1 = n_2 \lambda_2$

$\dfrac{n_1}{n_2} = \dfrac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1} = \dfrac{5000}{6000} = \dfrac{5}{6}$

For the minimum distance from the central maximum, we take the smallest integer values for $n_1$ and $n_2$, which are $n_1 = 5$ and $n_2 = 6$.

Substituting $n_1 = 5$ into the position formula:
$y = \dfrac{5 \times 6 \times 10^{-7} \times 2}{2 \times 10^{-3}}$

$y = 30 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}$

$y = 3 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 3\ \text{mm}$

Answer: $3\ \text{mm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When the un-polarised light beam is incident from air to glass $(n = 1.5)$ at the Brewster's angle,
options: reflected and refracted beams are partially polarized.
questions.solution:
According to Brewster's law, when an unpolarized light beam is incident on a transparent medium at the Brewster's angle, the reflected light is completely plane-polarized with its electric field vector perpendicular to the plane of incidence.

The refracted light remains partially polarized.

Therefore, the reflected beam is $100\ \%$ polarized.

Answer: reflected beam is polarized $100\ \%$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A parallel beam of light of intensity I is incident on a glass plate. $25\ \%$ of light is reflected by upper surface and $50\ \%$ of light is reflected from lower surface. Rest of the light is refracted. Above two reflected rays interfere, the ratio of maximum to minimum intensity in interference region is
questions.solution:
Let the intensity of the incident light be $I$.

Intensity of light reflected from the upper surface is:
$I_1 = 25\% \times I = \dfrac{I}{4}$

Intensity of light refracted into the glass plate is:
$I_t = I - \dfrac{I}{4} = \dfrac{3I}{4}$

At the lower surface, $50\%$ of this light is reflected. Thus, the intensity of light reflected from the lower surface is:
$I_2 = 50\% \times \dfrac{3I}{4} = \dfrac{3I}{8}$

This light emerges from the upper surface to interfere with the first reflected ray. Neglecting any further reflection at the upper boundary, the intensities of the two interfering rays are $I_1 = \dfrac{I}{4}$ and $I_2 = \dfrac{3I}{8}$.

The ratio of maximum to minimum intensity in the interference region is:
$\dfrac{I_{max}}{I_{min}} = \left( \dfrac{\sqrt{I_1} + \sqrt{I_2}}{\sqrt{I_1} - \sqrt{I_2}} \right)^2$

Substituting the values of $I_1$ and $I_2$:
$\dfrac{I_{max}}{I_{min}} = \left( \dfrac{\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{4}} + \sqrt{\dfrac{3I}{8}}}{\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{4}} - \sqrt{\dfrac{3I}{8}}} \right)^2 = \left( \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2} + \sqrt{\dfrac{3}{8}}}{\dfrac{1}{2} - \sqrt{\dfrac{3}{8}}} \right)^2$

Answer: $\left(\dfrac{\frac{1}{2} + \sqrt{\frac{3}{8}}}{\frac{1}{2} - \sqrt{\frac{3}{8}}}\right)^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A source of sound vibrating at frequency $500\ \text{Hz}$ is rotated in a circle of radius $\dfrac{100}{\pi}\ \text{cm}$ at a constant angular speed of $5$ revolutions per second. A listener is in the plane of the circle. The maximum and minimum frequency of sound heard are $\{$Speed of sound on air $= 332\ \text{m/s}\}$
questions.solution:
Given frequency of the source, $f_0 = 500\ \text{Hz}$

Radius of the circular path, $R = \dfrac{100}{\pi}\ \text{cm} = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\ \text{m}$

Angular speed, $\omega = 5\ \text{rev/s} = 5 \times 2\pi\ \text{rad/s} = 10\pi\ \text{rad/s}$

Linear speed of the source, $v_s = R\omega = \left(\dfrac{1}{\pi}\right)(10\pi) = 10\ \text{m/s}$

The maximum frequency is heard when the source moves directly towards the listener:

$f_{max} = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_s} \right)$

$f_{max} = 500 \left( \dfrac{332}{332 - 10} \right) = 500 \left( \dfrac{332}{322} \right) \approx 515.5\ \text{Hz} \approx 516\ \text{Hz}$

The minimum frequency is heard when the source moves directly away from the listener:

$f_{min} = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v}{v + v_s} \right)$

$f_{min} = 500 \left( \dfrac{332}{332 + 10} \right) = 500 \left( \dfrac{332}{342} \right) \approx 485.3\ \text{Hz} \approx 485\ \text{Hz}$

Answer: $516\ \text{Hz}$ and $485\ \text{Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Two sources of sound placed closed to each other, are emitting progressive waves given by
$y_1 = 4\sin(600\pi t)$ and $y_2 = 5\sin(608\pi t)$.
An observer located near these two sources of sound will hear
options: $4$ beats/s with intensity ratio $25 : 16$ between waxing and waning.
$8$ beats/s with intensity ratio $25 : 16$ between waxing and waning.
$8$ beats/s with intensity ratio $81 : 1$ between waxing and waning.
$4$ beats/s with intensity ratio $81 : 1$ between waxing and waning.
questions.solution:
The given equations of the progressive waves are:
$y_1 = 4\sin(600\pi t)$
$y_2 = 5\sin(608\pi t)$

Comparing these with the standard equation $y = A\sin(\omega t)$, we get the angular frequencies:
$\omega_1 = 600\pi \Rightarrow 2\pi f_1 = 600\pi \Rightarrow f_1 = 300$ Hz
$\omega_2 = 608\pi \Rightarrow 2\pi f_2 = 608\pi \Rightarrow f_2 = 304$ Hz

The beat frequency is the difference between the frequencies of the two waves:
$n = |f_1 - f_2| = |300 - 304| = 4$ beats/s

The amplitudes of the two waves are $A_1 = 4$ and $A_2 = 5$.
The maximum amplitude during waxing is $A_{max} = A_1 + A_2 = 4 + 5 = 9$.
The minimum amplitude during waning is $A_{min} = |A_1 - A_2| = |4 - 5| = 1$.

Since intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude ($I \propto A^2$), the intensity ratio between waxing and waning is:
$\dfrac{I_{max}}{I_{min}} = \left(\dfrac{A_{max}}{A_{min}}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{9}{1}\right)^2 = \dfrac{81}{1}$

Thus, the observer will hear $4$ beats/s with an intensity ratio of $81 : 1$.

Answer: $4$ beats/s with intensity ratio $81 : 1$ between waxing and waning.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform rope of length $L$ and mass $m_1$ hangs vertically from a rigid support. A block of mass $m_2$ is attached to the free end of the rope. A transverse pulse of wavelength $\lambda_1$ is produced at the lower end of the rope. The wavelength of the pulse when it reaches the top of the rope is $\lambda_2$. The ratio $\dfrac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}$ is
questions.solution:
The velocity of a transverse wave on a string is given by $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$, where $T$ is the tension and $\mu$ is the mass per unit length.

Since the frequency $f$ of the wave remains constant as it travels up the rope, the wavelength $\lambda$ is proportional to the wave velocity $v$. Thus, $\lambda \propto \sqrt{T}$.

At the lower end of the rope, the tension is due to the attached block of mass $m_2$.

$T_1 = m_2 g$

At the upper end of the rope, the tension is due to the mass of the rope and the attached block.

$T_2 = (m_1 + m_2) g$

The ratio of the wavelengths is given by:

$\dfrac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{(m_1 + m_2) g}{m_2 g}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_1 + m_2}{m_2}}$

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{m_1 + m_2}{m_2}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vibrating string of certain length $'l'$ under a tension $'T'$ resonates with a mode corresponding to the first overtone of an air column of length $75\ \text{cm}$ inside a tube closed at one end. The string also generates $4$ beats/s, when vibrated along with a tuning fork of frequency $'n'$. Increasing the tension of the string reduces the beat frequency. The frequency $'n'$ of the tuning fork in Hz is $\{$Velocity of sound in air is $340\ \text{m/s}\}$
questions.solution:
The frequency of the first overtone for an air column inside a tube closed at one end corresponds to the third harmonic, which is given by:

$f = \dfrac{3v}{4L}$

Substituting $v = 340\text{ m/s}$ and $L = 75\text{ cm} = 0.75\text{ m}$:

$f = \dfrac{3 \times 340}{4 \times 0.75} = 340\text{ Hz}$

Since the vibrating string resonates with this mode, the initial frequency of the string is $f_s = 340\text{ Hz}$.

The string produces $4\text{ beats/s}$ with a tuning fork of frequency $n$. Thus, the possible frequencies of the tuning fork are:

$n = f_s \pm 4$

$n = 340 + 4 = 344\text{ Hz}$ or $n = 340 - 4 = 336\text{ Hz}$

The frequency of a vibrating string is directly proportional to the square root of its tension, $f_s \propto \sqrt{T}$. Therefore, increasing the tension increases the frequency of the string ($f_s \gt 340\text{ Hz}$).

Since increasing the tension reduces the beat frequency, the frequency of the string must move closer to the frequency of the tuning fork. This is only possible if the frequency of the tuning fork is greater than the initial frequency of the string ($n \gt f_s$).

Hence, $n = 344\text{ Hz}$.
